chunks: Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿUmayr narrated from Abān ibn ʿUthmān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbdillāh, from Ḥumrān, who said:
I asked him about al-suknā and al-ʿumrā.

He said: “People are held to their conditions in this matter. If he stipulated it for his lifetime, then it is for his lifetime. And if it was for his descendants, then it is for his descendants as stipulated until they perish; then it is returned to the owner of the house.”

key_terms.السُّكْنَى: A granted right of residence or habitation in a property.
key_terms.الْعُمْرَى: A life estate-type grant tied to the lifetime of a person.
key_terms.شُرُوطِهِمْ: Their stipulated conditions, which determine the legal effect of the grant.
key_terms.صَاحِبِ الدَّارِ: The owner of the house to whom the property returns.
key_terms.لِعَقِبِهِ: For his descendants or offspring after him.

ai.seo_question: How does Shia fiqh rule on al-suknā and al-ʿumrā when conditions are attached to property use?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling on conditional property grants such as residential right and life estate. It states that such arrangements are governed by the conditions set by the grantor: if limited to a lifetime, they last for that lifetime, and if extended to descendants, they continue for them until their line ends, after which the property returns to the original owner.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.5598 - Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr narrated from Aban ibn Uthman from Abdur Rahman ibn Abi Abdullah from Humran who said:
I asked Imam (as) about Al-sukna (residential right) and Al-umra (life estate).

Imam (as) replied: "People are bound by their conditions. If he stipulated it for his lifetime, then it is for his lifetime. If he stipulated it for his descendants, then it is for his descendants as stipulated until they perish, after which it returns to the owner of the house."
